intrinsic_value_estimate: About $64 per share in the base case, range $42-$90. Method: owner earnings of ~$2.85/share (1988 net income $1,044.7M + D&A $169.8M + deferred tax $43.9M - capex $387M gives a floor of ~$865M; maintenance capex equal to depreciation gives ~$1,080M) projected 10 years. Base case: 11% EPS growth, as in 1978-88, then a 15x terminal multiple. Dividends start at $1.36 with ~42% payout. Discount rate is an assumed ~9% long bond yield, inferred from KO's own 9.25-12.4% coupons because the packet has no Treasury yield. Pessimistic case (8% growth, 12x) gives ~$42; management's mid-teens growth gives ~$90. Cross-check: affiliates are worth ~$2.2B (~$6/share), so the core business is priced at ~14.4x after-tax operating earnings, a ~6.9% earnings yield. Net working capital is only $1.06/share, so the framework's §5 net-NWC test fails by a wide margin.
margin_of_safety: About 27% below base-case value ($46.56 vs ~$64), ~48% against the mid-teens case, and negative (price ~10% above value) in the pessimistic case. Against the framework's only explicit §5 hurdle, buying below net working capital, there is no margin at all: the price is ~44x NWC and strict net-net value is negative. The margin rests on the franchise lasting, not on assets. Even the pessimistic case still returns ~8% a year with no permanent loss of capital.

key_reasons.reason: The core business earns exceptional returns on equity without depending on leverage or accounting gimmicks.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: 1988 ROE 33.3% (ar-1988); ~25% on net capital with net interest added back; soft-drink operating income $1,690.7M on $3,809M identifiable assets (~44% pre-tax); ROE was 20-23% in 1978-83 when debt was only 4-15% of capital.

key_reasons.reason: A measurable, widening moat: dominant share, rising margins and pricing discretion.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: ~45% world soft-drink share, up from <38% in 1980, more than double any competitor; US concentrate gross margin ~63%; consolidated gross margin 50.5% to 55.6% (1986-88); new CCE contracts allow pricing 'at its discretion' (ar-1986, ar-1988); international per-capita consumption only ~16% of the US level.

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are close to reported earnings, because the business needs little capital and passes cost increases through.
key_reasons.evidence: 1988 operating cash flow $1,166.8M against capex $387M; owner earnings ~$0.87-1.08B against net income $1,044.7M; management says the business 'has a low capital requirement and offers a high return on investment' and can 'adjust prices to compensate for increasing costs' (ar-1988).

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have created several times their value in market value, so the move to a 40% payout is justified.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: 1981-88: ~$6.46/share retained against a price gain from $11.13 to $44.63 (~$5.20 per $1 retained; ~$2.60 per $1 at a constant P/E).

key_reasons.reason: Able management in place is redeploying capital from low-return diversification back into the franchise and into share repurchases at sensible prices.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Honest, able management already in place; buybacks well below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1982, brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: Goizueta/Keough since 1981 with a 12% after-tax cost-of-capital hurdle; plastics, pasta and coffee sold, entertainment spun into a 49% affiliate; ~69M shares bought 1984-88 at ~$31.5 average, 1988 at ~$39.94 (~14x EPS); one-time items quantified per share in every report.

key_reasons.reason: The price is sensible for an outstanding business: it implies slower growth than the record, with a ~27% margin in the base case and no catalyst needed.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §6 No catalyst needed: the market eventually reflects business results (brk-letter-1987); 'outstanding business at a sensible price' (brk-letter-1987#18)
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 = 16.3x 1988 EPS of $2.85 (prices); EPS +17% in 1988 while the price is below the 1987 high of $53.13; the price implies only ~8-9% growth against 10.9% (1978-88) and 15.7% (1984-88) EPS growth.

key_reasons.reason: Concentration is warranted because the facts are clear and a drastic loss of value is unlikely; sizing below the 40% ceiling reflects currency, leverage and a moat-dependent margin.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §7 Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965); §9 avoid permanent loss of capital
key_reasons.evidence: Ten-year unbroken earnings record ($375M to $1,045M net income); consumers forced the return of the original formula as Coca-Cola classic, the top-selling US soft drink 1986-88; ~76% of operating income from outside the US; debt/capital 38.8%.

risks: The margin of safety depends on the moat lasting, not on assets; the framework's net-working-capital test fails completely, and the pessimistic case puts value (~$42) below the price.

Currency: ~76% of operating income is from outside the US, and recent growth was flattered by a 10-27% yearly rise in key currencies against the dollar; a stronger dollar would reduce reported earnings.
Leverage philosophy: a 35% net debt/net capital ceiling, debt-funded buybacks and $300M of money-market preferred conflict with the framework's preference for little or no debt.
Capital allocation drift: ~$1.9B in bottlers and Columbia Pictures earned only $48M of equity income in 1988; any return to diversification outside the core would destroy value.
Buybacks are justified by 'excess cash', not explicitly by a discount to intrinsic value; 1987 repurchases were made near ~18x earnings.
Promotional reporting and pay tied to the share price (8.66M options, cash awards on 855,000 share-equivalents) could pull management away from per-share value.
Inflation and economic distress in Latin America (volume fell in Brazil and Argentina in 1988), and contingent guarantees and recourse obligations (~$234M).
Gaps in the packet: no bond yield, no maintenance-capex split, no constant-currency figures, no proxy statement, and no direct knowledge of management.
what_would_change_my_mind: Constant-currency data showing international operating income growing only in line with volume, or a reversal of the concentrate margin expansion.
A long-term Treasury yield well above ~9%, which would lower value enough to remove the base-case margin.
Evidence that maintenance capex is well above depreciation, so owner earnings fall materially below reported earnings.
Management announcing a large acquisition outside soft drinks, or buybacks at prices well above intrinsic value.
Direct dealings with management that reveal a lack of candor or of owner orientation.
A price rise toward ~$64 before the position is built, which would remove the margin and stop further buying.
sell_triggers: Lasting erosion of the moat: world or US share falling for several years in a row, or concentrate gross margins contracting without a cost explanation.
Capital allocation turning hostile to owners: large diversifying acquisitions, issuing shares on unfavorable terms, or retained earnings no longer producing $1 of market value per $1 retained.
Leverage rising beyond management's own 35% ceiling to fund non-core uses.
Evidence that management is not honest or candid with owners.
Default is permanent holding: price alone is not a sell trigger, though a much better use of the capital could be weighed if the price reached an extreme multiple of owner earnings.
